title: metrics.stats (and call_logs.model_alias) keyed by the unresolved, length-unbounded client model string -> permanent unbounded growth
impact: One leaked gateway API key + a loop of `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"x-<counter>","messages":[]}` (each answered 404 in microseconds, unthrottled because the limiter runs later) permanently grows `mt.stats` by one 960-byte ModelStat plus an attacker-length string key per request; nothing is ever evicted, so the footprint is a monotonic high-water mark for the life of the process. Retention is amplified 3 ways: (a) every /metrics scrape re-serializes every key (see dos-2), (b) every such request also writes a call_logs row carrying the full raw string in an indexed column, so the SQLite file and its index grow at attacker-chosen rate and size, and (c) the same map is iterated by the admin /status page. Net effect is a slow, irreversible memory + disk exhaustion path that ends in OOM or a full-query collapse, and it cannot be mitigated by configuration because no bound exists on key count or key length.
recommendation: Three changes: (1) validate the client model string at parse time (reject >128 bytes / non `[A-Za-z0-9._:/\[\]-]`) in adapter.ParseRequest so no downstream consumer ever sees an unbounded token; (2) move `s.mx.Observe(...)` out of the pre-resolution defer and call it only after resolution, using the resolved alias, or bucket unresolved names into a single fixed key such as "__unknown__"; (3) bound the map: cap `len(mt.stats)` (e.g. 1024, evict/merge overflow into "__other__") and drop entries whose `lastSec` is >60s stale in the existing QPS() sweep (they already report 0 QPS, so eviction is loss-free). Truncate ModelAlias to 64 bytes before writeLog.
mitigations_checked: 16 MiB inbound body cap (gateway.go:322) bounds one key's size per request but not the count; gateway auth is required (gateway.go:215-221), so the attacker needs one valid API key; MaxConnections (gateway.go:195) limits concurrency, not the cumulative key set; ErrorEvent ring IS bounded (metrics.go:77-79 `if len(mt.recent) > 50 {`); slb.rr cursors ARE pruned (slb.go:213-217) - no equivalent for stats; the guard/quota/rate-limit steps do not run on this path, so they provide no protection.

title: Unauthenticated /metrics renders O(N) attacker-inflated stats while holding the same mutex every gateway request takes -> lock starvation
evidence: /metrics has no auth by explicit design - routes.go:19-24: `// ... 故不做 JWT 鉴权` followed by `r.GET("/metrics", func(c *gin.Context) {` ... `s.mx.WritePromRender(c.Writer, s)`. The render path takes a lock and iterates the whole stats map while holding it: metrics.go:88-100 `func (mt *Metrics) QPS() []QPSInfo {` / `mt.mu.Lock()` / `defer mt.mu.Unlock()` / `for m, s := range mt.stats {` / `s.rotate(time.Now().Unix())` ... (rotate at metrics.go:16-33 does up to 59 iterations of two 60-element array copies). That same `mt.mu` is the mutex every gateway request takes at least three times: metrics.go:114 `func (mt *Metrics) ConnInc() { mt.mu.Lock(); mt.conns++; mt.mu.Unlock() }`, 115-121 ConnDec, 122 `func (mt *Metrics) Conns() int64 { mt.mu.Lock(); ...`, plus Observe/RecordError - reached from gateway.go:195 (`int64(snap.General.MaxConnections) > 0 && s.mx.Conns() >= int64(snap.General.MaxConnections)`), gateway.go:300-301 and gateway.go:318. prom.go:112-114 (`func (mt *Metrics) WritePromRender(...) { mt.promMu.Lock(); defer mt.promMu.Unlock()`) only serializes scrapes; it does not shorten the mt.mu hold, and each queued scrape keeps its handler goroutine + connection alive. prom.go:135-139 emits HELP+TYPE+sample twice per key, so the response body is O(N x len(key)) too. Extra evidence that N is reachable from the inside: dashboard/status calls the same O(N) render from an authenticated poll that the shipped SPA runs every 5s (backend/internal/admin/dashboard.go:137 `"qps_by_model":  s.mx.QPS(),` with frontend/src/pages/settings/RuntimeStatus.tsx:34 `refetchInterval: 5000,`).
impact: dos-1 gives an attacker a permanent, cheap knob for N. A single unauthenticated client then loops `GET /metrics` (no key, no rate limit, no connection cap on this route since MaxConnections is only counted inside Handle) and holds `mt.mu` for O(N) each time. At N = 10^5 stale keys the hold is tens of milliseconds per scrape, which at scrape-per-response loop rate is a ~100% duty cycle on the global mutex, so *every* gateway request blocks in ConnInc/Conns/Observe: the whole data plane stalls to a crawl while the process looks healthy (CPU low, no errors). Concurrently, /metrics responses themselves become multi-MB (26 MB+ at 100k x 30-byte keys), and because no server read/write deadline exists (dos-4) a slow-reading scraper pins handler goroutines and sockets indefinitely -> goroutine/fd pileup. Also leaks the entire historical model namespace (including private/implicit upstream model names used as keys) to unauthenticated callers.
recommendation: Decouple the render lock from the collection lock: take mt.mu only to snapshot (m, total, errs) into a slice, release, then format. Give QPS() a hard output cap (top-K by QPS plus an aggregate bucket) and skip entries whose 60s windows are all zero. Add a cardinality ceiling on Prometheus label values (truncate to e.g. 64 bytes) so response size cannot be inflated. Require a token/mTLS or at minimum bind /metrics to an internal interface, and add a per-endpoint concurrency limit / ReadHeaderTimeout so scrapes cannot pile up.
mitigations_checked: promMu serializes scrapes (prom.go:113) but this *increases* goroutine pileup rather than bounding it; rotate() self-clears when shift >= 60 (metrics.go:21-23) so old windows read zero - that makes eviction safe but does not free the entry; TRUSTED_PROXIES/XFF is irrelevant here (no IP-based control on /metrics at all); the endpoint is a plain text writer with no body reading, so no inbound-size limit applies.

title: runStreamGuardCheck re-scans the entire accumulated stream at every threshold crossing: O(L^2) byte-work x K rules with a fresh ToLower(text) allocation per rule, on one connection
evidence:
The stream loop checks on every threshold crossing but always hands the WHOLE accumulated text to the engine:
			if snap.General.GuardEnabled && snap.Output.Enabled && acc.Len() >= nextCheck {
				stop, fatal := s.runStreamGuardCheck(snap, sw, reqID, ap, acc.String())
... (gateway.go:699-700), and the advance is additive: gateway.go:708 `nextCheck += threshold`. The threshold defaults to 256 bytes (settings.go:62 `StreamChunkThreshold: 256`) with a floor of 64 (gateway.go:633 `if threshold < 64 {` / 634 `threshold = 256`). runStreamGuardCheck then re-scans from offset 0: gateway.go:777 `vd := guard.CheckOutput(snap, text)`. There is no Aho-Corasick automaton or any shared scan - CheckOutput is a per-rule linear loop (engine.go:136-152) and each 'contains' rule lowercases the entire text again: engine.go:204 `return strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(text), strings.ToLower(kw.Raw.Word))`, plus a full-text regex ReplaceAllString per mask rule (engine.go:150 `vd.Text = r.Re.ReplaceAllString(vd.Text, repl)`). Rule count K is unbounded: admin/guard.go:116-124 and 161-190 create one row per imported record with no cap, and manager.go:276-291 compiles them all. The stream is also unbounded in L: gateway.go:492-505 deliberately applies no timeout for streams (`ctx := c.Request.Context()` only inside `if !cr.Stream {`), and client `max_tokens` is taken verbatim and never capped (gateway.go:365-369 only injects a default when the field is absent). The end-of-stream path repeats the same whole-text work: gateway.go:749-750 `if !stopped && ... && acc.Len() > 0 { if _, fatal := s.runStreamGuardCheck(..., acc.String()); fatal {`, plus more full copies at 755 `usage = estimateUsage(usage, ap.input, acc.String())` and 759 `ap.output = guard.MaskForLog(snap, acc.String())`.
impact: Total byte-work per stream is ~K x L^2/(2 x threshold). With shipped defaults (threshold 256) and a modest 1 MiB completion at K=10 keywords, that is ~4095 checks averaging 0.5 MiB -> ~2 GiB scanned and ~2 GiB of freshly allocated lowercase garbage per keyword, i.e. ~20 GiB of byte-ops and allocations for ONE response. A single authenticated API key needs one connection and no concurrency: it asks a reasoning-style model to chatter (or points a provider at an attacker-controlled upstream that streams forever), and the gateway burns CPU/GC on the request goroutine until the process OOMs or starves every other tenant. Because the SSE writer flushes per delta (adapter/sse.go:228-240), the attack is fully observable as latency growth on all other requests long before it is diagnosed.
recommendation: Scan only the new segment per check and keep a tail overlap of max(pattern length)-1 bytes (track a scanned-offset cursor instead of passing acc.String()); build one Aho-Corasick automaton per snapshot at reload time so a scan is O(L + matches) independent of K; cap the number of guard rules per snapshot (e.g. 2000) and the number of bytes any single stream will scan (after the cap, log-and-continue rather than re-scan); stop copying `acc` (use acc.Len()/byte reads over the builder or a ring buffer); and enforce a server-side max on client max_tokens per alias.
mitigations_checked: engine.go:130-134 recovers panics and fails open (so a bad rule cannot crash, but also cannot stop the scan); guard only runs when GuardEnabled && Output.Enabled, both default true (settings.go:32, 61); the `replace` strategy terminates the stream after the first hit (gateway.go:797-805), which limits L in that mode - the `log`/`block` strategies and non-matching output do not terminate, so the quadratic cost is fully paid; tool-call text appended at 735-745 also adds to L; audit text is truncated to 4000 bytes (engine.go:189-191), so truncation exists post-hoc but not before the scan.

title: Configured inbound timeouts are never applied to the HTTP server: no ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/IdleTimeout/MaxHeaderBytes on any route
evidence: main.go:126 is the only server construction: `srv := &http.Server{Addr: fmt.Sprintf(":%d", cfg.ListenPort), Handler: engine}` - no timeout fields at all. config.go:72-73 computes `90 * time.Second` for ReadTimeout and `0` for WriteTimeout, but grep for `ReadTimeout` across backend shows the only hits are unrelated client/redis options (quota/redis_limiter.go:47, slb/slb.go:79, admin/redis_mfa.go:73) plus the struct declaration (config.go:25-26) - cfg.ReadTimeout and cfg.WriteTimeout are never read anywhere, so the 90s intent is dead code. There is no `SetReadDeadline`, `http.TimeoutHandler`, or MaxHeaderBytes anywhere in the repo (grep: 0 non-test hits). Consequences on the gateway path: the whole request body is read with no deadline at gateway.go:322 `body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(c.Request.Body, 16<<20))` (and gateway.go:98 for count_tokens); the concurrency guard only counts handlers, and only after auth (gateway.go:195 check, gateway.go:300 `s.mx.ConnInc()`), so a connection stalled in header/body reading is invisible to MaxConnections; and gateway.go:492-505 gives streams no total or idle timeout.
impact: Fully unauthenticated, near-zero-cost outage: (a) Slowloris - send header bytes at 1 byte/10s and hold sockets; nothing is ever reaped because ReadHeaderTimeout and IdleTimeout are both 0 and keep-alives never expire, so the process exhausts file descriptors / goroutine stacks with no counter and no log. (b) Light-hour body attack - trickle a 16 MiB JSON body; each request pins a handler goroutine plus a 16 MiB ReadAll buffer for hours, so a few hundred sockets is multi-GB RSS. (c) Slow-reader - a client that never reads the response blocks the relay writes (sse.go:234-240 raw write + Flush) forever, since WriteTimeout is 0 AND never set on the server, which is the mechanism that lets one key permanently occupy MaxConnections (dos-9). The stated design fact 'WriteTimeout=0 intentional for SSE; non-stream bounded' does not hold inbound: the non-stream bound (DefaultTimeoutSeconds) is applied only to the *upstream* context (gateway.go:497-505), never to reading from or writing to the client.
recommendation: Apply the timeouts that are already configured: `ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second, ReadTimeout: cfg.ReadTimeout (90s), IdleTimeout: 120s, MaxHeaderBytes: 1<<20`. For SSE, keep server-level WriteTimeout=0 but set a per-write deadline on the hijacked/flush path (e.g. `c.Request.Context()` plus `http.NewResponseController(w).SetWriteDeadline(time.Now().Add(30s))` refreshed on each flush, and an equivalent idle/read-timeout on the upstream body). Wrap body reads in a context deadline (e.g. 30s to read 16 MiB) so trickle clients are cut, and count connection reservations before the body read so the overload guard actually covers this phase.
mitigations_checked: gin.Recovery (main.go:95) prevents panics but not pileups; srv.Shutdown with a 5s ctx (main.go:157-161) works only for graceful exit; the listen-retry loop (main.go:130-151) rebinds but does not drain stuck conns; per-request upstream ctx cancel (gateway.go:496, 503) does bound upstream reads for non-stream responses; TRUSTED_PROXIES empty means ClientIP is the TCP peer, so source-based mitigation is possible but not implemented (no connection cap per IP anywhere).

title: Quota is check-then-consume with the consume after the upstream round trip: overshoot up to MaxConnections x unbounded tokens, and aborted/errored streams are never metered at all
evidence: Check is a pure read with no reservation: quota.go:158 `qm.db.Where("id IN ? AND enabled = ?", ids, true).Find(&rows)` and quota.go:173 `if r.LimitValue > 0 && used >= r.LimitValue {`. It is called mid-pipeline at gateway.go:419 `if ok3, over := s.qm.Check(snap, apiKey.ID, ap.alias); !ok3 {`, while the increment happens only after the response is fully relayed: gateway.go:614 `s.qm.Consume(snap, ap.keyID, ap.alias, usage.Prompt, usage.Completion)` and gateway.go:768 (same call) - guarded by gateway.go:767 `if ap.status == "ok" || ap.status == "blocked" {`. Consume itself has a second, non-atomic reset branch at quota.go:196-198: `if now.After(q.ResetAt) {` ... `"used_value": delta, "reset_at": NextReset(q.Period, now)})` (an assignment, not an increment).
impact: The TOCTOU window is the whole upstream round trip - up to DefaultTimeoutSeconds=120s for non-stream (gateway.go:498, settings.go:31) and unbounded for streams (gateway.go:492-505). Every request in flight when used == limit-1 is admitted, so a key whose quota is 1 request/day can spend ~MaxConnections=1000 requests (settings.go:32, the only admission control) in one burst; for token quotas the per-request delta is itself attacker-shaped because client max_tokens is not capped and streams are unbounded, so overshoot is effectively unlimited (1000 concurrent full-length completions billed to the operator). Worse, the control is not merely overshootable but bypassable: any stream that ends in a read error returns frFatal at gateway.go:726 with ap.status = "error", which fails the gateway.go:767 test, so the generated tokens are never added to used_value - an attacker loops 'start a large completion, disconnect at N KB' and consumes provider budget forever with a permanently empty quota counter. Finally, N concurrent requests that all take the expired-cycle branch overwrite each other (used_value = delta), so the counter under-counts even for successful traffic.
recommendation: Reserve before forwarding: an atomic `UPDATE quotas SET used_value = used_value + :est WHERE id = ? AND (used_value + :est) <= limit_value` (estimate from the request body via tokens.Count) executed in the same step as Check, then reconcile the reservation with the real delta in Consume; make the lazy-reset branch an increment (`used_value = delta` only inside a `WHERE used_value = 0` guard or a transaction). Meter aborted streams too - call Consume with the accumulated usage on the scanner.Err()/early-return paths, since the upstream already produced and billed those tokens. Cap client max_tokens against an operator-set alias ceiling.
mitigations_checked: the increment form at quota.go:201 `UpdateColumn("used_value", gorm.Expr("used_value + ?", delta))` is atomic in SQL (no read-modify-write in Go) for the non-reset branch; Check re-reads live DB values instead of trusting the snapshot (quota.go:158), so cross-restart persistence is fine; requests with delta <= 0 are skipped (quota.go:192-194); degrade-on-exceed (gateway.go:421-427) reduces cost but still admits unlimited requests to the degraded alias because the alias switch happens after Check and the new alias is never re-checked; there is no per-request or per-connection cost ceiling anywhere.

title: Guard rails, not throttles: the 16 MiB body read, JSON decode and full per-message guard scan all run before the rate limiter and quota are consulted
evidence: Order inside Handle: gateway.go:322 reads up to `16<<20` bytes; gateway.go:328 `cr, err := adapter.ParseRequest(clientProto, body)` decodes it (twice over for nested payloads - parseOpenAIChat unmarshals body then unmarshals `raw.Messages` again at adapter.go:136); gateway.go:381-395 runs the guard over *every message* (`for i := range cr.Messages {` / `vd := guard.CheckInput(snap, cr.Messages[i].Content)`) and gateway.go:398 `ap.input = guard.MaskForLog(snap, cr.InputPlainText())` concatenates and regex-replaces the whole prompt; only then does gateway.go:410 `if ok2, hit := s.rl.Allow(snap, apiKey.ID, ap.alias); !ok2 {` run, followed by gateway.go:419 for quota. The limiter is also opt-in per rule: quota.go:55-80 iterates `snap.RateLimits` and returns `true, nil` when nothing matches, and settings.EnsureDefaults (settings.go:127-157) seeds no rate-limit rule or quota row at all, so a default deployment has zero request-rate throttling on the data plane. The rate check itself is a fixed window with a burst-then-reject shape (quota.go:69-77, `w.count++` before comparing), so a window boundary admits up to 2x MaxRequests back-to-back.
impact: The throttle protects the wrong thing. Everything expensive-per-byte - 16 MiB kernel->user copy, two JSON decodes, K-linear scan over the whole prompt with per-rule allocations (see dos-3), InputPlainText concatenation, PII ReplaceAllString over the full text - is spent before any counter is consulted, so a client can drive that cost at line rate and only be stopped afterwards (or never, if no rule exists, or immediately on the unthrottled 404 path of dos-1). Concretely, with a configured rule of 5 req/60s the attacker still gets 5 x 16 MiB parses + guard scans per minute per key with no protection against the burst, and unauthenticated-but-key-holding clients get an unthrottled 404 path for free.
recommendation: Move a per-API-key always-on token bucket (a sane default such as 20 rps burst 40) to immediately after AuthMiddleware, before the body read; keep the alias-scoped rule evaluation where it is. Add a Content-Length pre-check and use `http.MaxBytesReader` so oversize bodies fail during read instead of after, and stream-parse (json.Decoder with a token limit) rather than ReadAll+Unmarshal. Also apply a cheap global body-throughput cap (bytes/sec) that does not require configuration.
mitigations_checked: MaxConnections is checked pre-handler (gateway.go:195) so per-request cost is concurrency-bounded; auth (SHA-256 map lookup, gateway.go:215) and the IP allowlist (gateway.go:222) run first, so anonymous clients cannot reach the expensive code; gateway.go:370 `if !apiKey.AllowsModel(cr.Model)` rejects unauthorized aliases before the guard; CountTokens has its own 16 MiB cap (gateway.go:98) but no limiter/quota at all (it returns before step 3).

title: audit.Logger queue-full fallback performs a synchronous SQLite INSERT on the request path - a positive-feedback collapse under load
evidence: audit.go:37-47: `func (l *Logger) Write(cl *model.CallLog) {` ... `select {` / `case l.ch <- cl:` / `default:` / `l.db.Create(cl)` - the overflow branch writes on the caller's goroutine, and its result is discarded (no log, unlike the batch path which logs at audit.go:68 `log.Printf("[audit] batch insert failed: %v", err)`). Queue depth is 4096 (audit.go:24 `ch: make(chan *model.CallLog, 4096)`). The consumer is one goroutine that batches at most 64 rows per transaction with a 200 ms tick (audit.go:60 `ticker := time.NewTicker(200 * time.Millisecond)`, 62 `batch := make([]*model.CallLog, 0, 64)`, 67 `if err := l.db.CreateInBatches(batch, 50).Error; err != nil {`, 79-81 flush at 64). The caller is the gateway request goroutine: writeLog ends in `s.auditLog.Write(cl)` (gateway.go:280), invoked from the defer registered at gateway.go:314-319 - i.e. after the response bytes are written but before `defer s.mx.ConnDec()` (registered earlier at gateway.go:301) runs, so the MaxConnections slot is still held during the synchronous insert.
impact: Sustained load above the batched writer's drain rate (~64 rows/transaction; with the single-connection SQLite pool of dos-8, a few hundred rows/s at best) fills 4096 slots in seconds, then every request pays an extra unbatched INSERT of an ~8 KB row (input_text + output_text are unbounded TEXT, model.go:256-257) serialized behind the same one connection - which further slows the batch writer, so the system latches into the slow path and stays there. The visible symptom is gateway-wide 503 'too many connections' (gateway.go:196-198) plus an unexplained audit hole (failures are silent, a compliance impact for the audit feature). Also note the retention sweeper (audit.go:89-105, hourly `DELETE ... WHERE created_at < ?` over the same single conn) periodically monopolizes the pool.
recommendation: Never block or write synchronously on the request path: on queue overflow, increment a dropped/overflow counter and hand the row to a bounded overflow ring drained by a separate goroutine (or append to a local JSONL file for later replay), and surface queue depth + drops in /metrics and /status. If a synchronous fallback must remain, put it behind a semaphore of 1 with a short timeout so it cannot fan out across 1000 handlers. Raise the batch ceiling and/or flush on size as well as time, and log the fallback error.
mitigations_checked: the WebSocket fan-out is genuinely non-blocking and slow-consumer-dropping (hub.go:48-58 with `default:` / `h.drop++`, buffer 64 at hub.go:13), and its payloads are small because CallLog hides InputText/OutputText/GuardFindings from JSON (model.go:256-257, 267 `json:"-"`) - so the hub is not a memory sink; audit volume can be reduced by CallAuditOnlyErrors/CallAuditSampling (gateway.go:253-267), but both default to record-everything (settings.go:33 `CallAuditEnabled: true, CallAuditSampling: 1`) and error/blocked rows are always written, which is the path dos-1/dos-3 let an attacker pump.

title: Per-request synchronous writes on a single-connection SQLite pool: quota Consume plus a redundant settings SELECT per matched quota on the hot path (Snapshot.Alerts exists but is unused)
evidence: Consume issues 2 DB statements per matched quota, on the request goroutine: quota.go:184 `for _, q := range matchQuotas(snap, apiKeyID, alias) {` then either quota.go:197 `qm.db.Model(&model.Quota{}).Where("id = ?", q.ID).Updates(map[string]any{` or 200-201 `UpdateColumn("used_value", gorm.Expr("used_value + ?", delta))`, and unconditionally quota.go:203 `qm.maybeAlert(q, delta)` which re-reads configuration from the DB every single request: quota.go:210 `_ = settings.LoadKV(qm.db, model.SetKeyQuotaAlert, &s, settings.DefaultQuotaAlerts())` (a SELECT + json.Unmarshal inside the per-quota loop). All of that contends on one connection: db.go:50-52 `if strings.ToLower(dbType) == "sqlite" {` / `sqlDB.SetMaxOpenConns(1) // 避免 sqlite 写锁竞争（WAL 下读仍并发）` - with MaxOpenConns(1) nothing is concurrent, and database/sql queues waiters without bound or timeout. Check (quota.go:158) adds another SELECT per request. Same pattern elsewhere on the path: gateway.go:247 `s.db.Model(&model.APIKey{}).Where("id = ?", id).Update("last_used_at", &t)` (throttled to 1/min/key by gateway.go:236), plus the audit INSERTs of dos-7, and the hourly cleanup DELETE (audit.go:102-103).
impact: Process-wide throughput is capped by writes x 1 connection, so modest authenticated traffic (a few hundred rps with 2-3 quotas attached to a key -> 5-8 statements each) saturates the pool; request goroutines then queue inside database/sql while holding MaxConnections slots, producing gateway-wide latency spikes and 503s with idle CPU. Two amplifiers: (a) maybeAlert's stale comparison against snapshot data (quota.go:214-215 `before := float64(q.UsedValue) / float64(q.LimitValue) * 100`) can be true for every request while the DB counter climbs, spawning one detached webhook POST per request (quota.go:222 `go postWebhook(s.WebhookURL, payload)`) - an attacker-driven outbound flood + goroutine pileup against the configured endpoint; (b) `snap.Alerts` is already loaded on the snapshot (manager.go:340) yet never read (grep: only manager.go:340 and a test reference), so the per-request SELECT is pure avoidable overhead.
recommendation: Read alert configuration from the snapshot (`snap.Alerts`) instead of LoadKV per request; accumulate quota deltas in memory and flush on the existing 1-minute tick like FlushHits (quota.go:83-92) or batch them; coalesce maybeAlert with a per-quota in-flight flag/edge detector keyed off the flushed value. Raise SetMaxOpenConns for WAL reads (and set `_busy_timeout`), or move write-only work to a dedicated writer goroutine. Bound webhook fan-out with a semaphore plus a min-interval per quota.
mitigations_checked: postWebhook is detached with a 5s context (quota.go:231-232) and uses http.DefaultClient, so it cannot stall the handler directly; LoadKV errors are ignored and `!s.Enabled` short-circuits at quota.go:211-213 (DefaultQuotaAlerts has Enabled:false, settings.go:75), so the default configuration only pays the SELECT; delta <= 0 skips the write (quota.go:192-194); the StartBackground reset job is single-ticker (quota.go:244-264) with no pileup.

title: MaxConnections is a global, checked-then-incremented counter with no per-key concurrency limit: one API key can own all 1000 slots with never-timed-out streams
evidence: gateway.go:195-200 is the only admission control: `if int64(snap.General.MaxConnections) > 0 && s.mx.Conns() >= int64(snap.General.MaxConnections) {` -> 503 `too_many_connections`. It is a check in AuthMiddleware against a counter that is incremented later, inside Handle (gateway.go:300 `s.mx.ConnInc()` / 301 `defer s.mx.ConnDec()`), so concurrent requests race past the boundary; and when the setting is 0 or negative the guard is disabled entirely. The value is shared globally - nothing in the file tracks concurrency per API key, per IP, or per upstream (quota.RateLimiter counts request rate in a fixed window, not in-flight work, quota.go:55-80). Slot release is not time-bounded for streams: gateway.go:492-505 deliberately applies a timeout only `if !cr.Stream {`, and combined with dos-4 (no server write deadline) a client that stops reading keeps `sw.Delta`/`sw.raw` blocked (adapter/sse.go:234-240 `_, err := io.WriteString(s.w, line)` / `s.flush()`) forever.
impact: Cross-tenant denial of the whole data plane with one API key and no CPU cost: open 1000 concurrent `"stream": true` requests (optionally to a slow upstream, or simply never read the socket) and every other key in the deployment gets 503, while the gateway reports healthy. The unthrottled 404/metrics path (dos-1) and the never-metered stream path (dos-5) mean the attacker need not pay quota at all to hold slots. Because slots are released only when the relay finishes, a single long-lived client is enough; there is no reaper and no idle timeout.
recommendation: Add per-key and per-source-IP in-flight limits (e.g. max 32 concurrent streams per key) alongside the global cap; reserve/release the counter with an atomic CAS around the check (or use a semaphore) instead of check-then-inc; add an idle/no-progress timeout on the SSE relay (e.g. 60s without upstream bytes) and a max stream duration per alias; treat MaxConnections=0 as 'use default' rather than 'unlimited' or document it loudly.
mitigations_checked: streams do abort when the client disconnects, because the upstream request carries `c.Request.Context()` (gateway.go:496, 515 `req = req.WithContext(ctx)`), so a *gone* client frees its slot; the failover retry sleep is bounded by the number of upstreams, not by RetryCount alone (gateway.go:447-471 with the `tried` map); resp bodies are closed (gateway.go:524) and error bodies are capped at 64 KiB (gateway.go:530); upstream client transport pools connections (gateway.go:58-60, MaxIdleConns 200/PerHost 64) but sets no MaxConnsPerHost and no ResponseHeaderTimeout.

title: slb.Balancer holds its single global mutex across blocking Redis round trips on the request path and inside /metrics rendering
evidence: Pick takes the one global mutex for its whole body (slb.go:223-224 `bl.mu.Lock()` / `defer bl.mu.Unlock()`) and then performs network I/O under it: slb.go:246-248 `if len(tried) == 0 && bl.rdb != nil && !bl.redisDown.get() {` / `if picked, ok := bl.swrrRemote(alias, candidates); ok {`, where swrr_remote.go:61-63 is a live Lua EVAL with `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 300*time.Millisecond)` ... `res, err := swrrScript.Run(ctx, bl.rdb, ...)`. The same lock also covers the breaker health read, which can itself call Redis: slb.go:176-178 (`b.remoteCheckedAt = now` / `b.remoteOpenUntilMS = bl.remoteOpen(id)` - throttled to <=1/s *per provider*) reached from Pick at slb.go:234. Worst case is the scrape path: HealthList takes bl.mu (slb.go:348-349) and for every provider that has no local breaker performs an *unthrottled* Redis GET inside the loop - slb.go:359 `} else if openMS := bl.remoteOpen(id); openMS > 0 && time.Now().UnixMilli() < openMS {` - called from admin/prom.go:19 `if st := s.mgr.Get(); st != nil {` / `for _, h := range s.bl.HealthList(st) {`, i.e. from the unauthenticated /metrics handler (routes.go:21).
impact: Redis becomes a gateway-wide serialization point. With REDIS_ADDR configured (mysql/pg deployments) and Redis degraded-but-reachable (e.g. ~250 ms latency, below the 300 ms timeout, so no degradation flag is ever set), each Pick can hold bl.mu for up to 300 ms, collapsing data-plane throughput to a few requests per second for all keys at once; a Pick whose alias has several unhealthy providers adds up to providers x 300 ms. An unauthenticated GET /metrics storm adds O(providers) x 300 ms holds of the same mutex per scrape (PoolSize 20 means the 1000 handler goroutines queue inside go-redis). Failures are worse: each error sets redisDown and spawns another watcher (slb.go:126, 146, 159; swrr_remote.go:67 `go bl.watchRedis()`), so repeated degrade/recover cycles leak 5s-sleeping goroutines.
recommendation: Never do Redis I/O under bl.mu: read breaker/cursor state into a value under the lock, release, then I/O; or move shared state to a background refresher publishing atomic snapshots (like the runtime.Snapshot pattern already used for config). Apply the same <=1/s/provider throttle in HealthList. Cache the last successful remoteOpen value so a degraded Redis costs at most one throttled probe rather than a locked round trip, and guard watchRedis/watchRecovery with a CAS so only one watcher exists.
mitigations_checked: all Redis calls carry 300-500 ms contexts (slb.go:78-80, 117, 141, 156; swrr_remote.go:61) so a hold is finite; `bl.redisDown.get()` short-circuits the remote path after the first error (slb.go:114, 165-188, 246) and Pick falls back to the local cursor (slb.go:251); the health-probe loop is separate and bounded (health.go:26 `const defaultConcurrent = 8`, 72 sem, 38 `client: &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}`, sequential rounds via wg.Wait at health.go:88) - I specifically checked 'health probe pileup' and found NO gap there (Go tickers drop, ProbeAll cannot overlap itself, and concurrency is capped at 8); Redis limiter keys self-expire via PEXPIRE (redis_limiter.go:66-72), so that limiter has no map leak.

title: Every config reload re-exports the whole configuration from the DB and writes it as a JSON blob, so Bump storms cost O(config) table scans + writes per admin write
evidence: Reload unconditionally ends in version recording: manager.go:365-366 `m.cur.Store(snap)` / `m.recordVersion(snap, status, errMsg, reason)`, and recordVersion discards the snapshot it was handed and re-reads everything: manager.go:384 `bundle := m.exportBundleFrom(snap)`, where bundle.go:70 `func (m *Manager) exportBundleFrom(_ *Snapshot) *ConfigBundle {` (parameter ignored) calls ExportBundle, i.e. 8 full-table reads plus a Preload (bundle.go:30-66: `m.db.Find(&b.Providers)`, `m.db.Preload("Upstreams").Find(&b.Aliases)`, `... b.Keywords`, `b.PIIRules`, `b.Injection`, `b.Quotas`, `b.RateLimits`, `b.APIKeys`, `m.db.Find(&sets)`). That bundle is marshalled and inserted as one row: manager.go:386-391 `if b, err := json.Marshal(bundle); err == nil {` / `sj = string(b)` / `m.db.Create(&ver)` - and ConfigVersion.SnapshotJSON has no size bound (model.go:230 `SnapshotJSON string`). Then 4 more log writes, each doing its own prune query (manager.go:398-404 -> logLoad at 414-421, `m.db.Model(&model.ConfigLoadLog{}).Order("id desc").Offset(200).Limit(500).Pluck("id", &drop)`), plus a read-modify-write of config_meta at 406-411. Reload is triggered per admin write by Bump (manager.go:130-137, called from e.g. admin/guard.go:59, 86, 99, 126, 192, and admin/settings.go:36) and Bump's counter update is a non-transactional LoadKV/SaveKV pair; because dbCount is deliberately written back as the *starting* counter (manager.go:359 `m.dbCount = dbCountAtStart`), a burst of K bumps produces K more full reloads rather than one.
impact: Config churn is quadratic in config size: with a keyword set of 50k rows (~10 MB of JSON - nothing caps rule count; admin/guard.go:116-124/161-190 create one row per record with no limit), every single admin edit re-reads 10 MB, marshals 10 MB, and writes a 10 MB row, ~50 of which are retained (manager.go:393 `Offset(50).Limit(500)`), i.e. 500 MB of near-duplicate blobs in the same SQLite file that also holds the call audit - and every one of those operations is serialized on the single gateway DB connection (db.go:52), competing with the per-request quota/audit writes of dos-7/dos-8. An admin script (or the UI's per-keystroke save) clicking through a few hundred edits is enough to stall the data plane; an operator with disk quotas gets a full 'database is locked'/out-of-disk outage. Reload's regex compilation (manager.go:280-321) additionally re-compiles every pattern per reload, so reload latency itself grows linearly with K.
recommendation: Serialize the version bundle from the in-memory snapshot that was just built (or diff against the previous bundle and store incremental rows), run recordVersion on a bounded background worker, and skip version recording when nothing but the counter changed. Cap total guard rules per snapshot, and cap/prune SnapshotJSON (e.g. store a checksum + gzip, keep 10 versions). Make Bump's counter increment an atomic SQL `counter = counter + 1` inside the caller's transaction.
mitigations_checked: concurrent reloads are collapsed by the busy CAS (manager.go:191-193 `if !m.busy.CompareAndSwap(false, true) {` / `return nil`), the trigger channel has capacity 1 (manager.go:100) so pending events coalesce, the poll interval floor is 1s (manager.go:169-175), the swap is atomic so in-flight requests never block on config reload (manager.go:365), versions are pruned to 50 and load logs to 200, and batch admin operations issue one Bump per call (admin/guard.go:126) rather than per item.

title: RateLimiter.windows entries are never evicted (no TTL sweep), leaving permanent per-(rule,key,alias) state after rules/keys/aliases are deleted
evidence: quota.go:38-43 declares `windows map[string]*window // key = ruleID:apiKeyID:alias` and 67-72 inserts on first use: `key := fmt.Sprintf("%d:%d:%s", r.ID, apiKeyID, alias)` / `if !ok || now.After(w.resetAt) {` / `w = &window{count: 0, resetAt: now.Add(time.Duration(max1(r.WindowSeconds)) * time.Second)}` / `rl.windows[key] = w`. Expired windows are replaced in place but nothing is ever deleted - repo-wide grep for `delete(rl.windows` -> 0 hits - and no sweeper exists in the package; the only periodic job (quota.go:83-92 FlushHits) resets `rl.hits` but leaves `rl.windows` untouched. RedisLimiter has no equivalent problem because its keys carry PEXPIRE (redis_limiter.go:66-72).
impact: Slow, configuration-bounded growth: one `window` (~40 B plus the key string) per historical (rule, apikey, alias) triple that is never reused after deletion, so a tenant-management workflow that churns API keys/aliases/rules leaks monotonically for the process lifetime, and Allow()'s map grows the same way. Not attacker-controllable: `alias` here is the post-resolution name (gateway.go:410 passes ap.alias, which by that point must exist in snap.Aliases or snap.UpstreamModels), and rule/APIKey IDs come from the admin DB. Reported as hygiene/defense-in-depth; the fix is trivial and also closes the case where a stale `resetAt` far in the future keeps counting against a re-created rule ID.
recommendation: Prune expired windows on the existing minute tick (FlushHits already holds the same mutex): iterate and `delete(rl.windows, k)` where `now.After(w.resetAt)` and the entry was not touched in the last cycle; alternatively key the map by a rule `updated_at`/generation so stale generations become garbage immediately. Add a defensive hard cap on len(windows) with an alert when exceeded.
mitigations_checked: keys are bounded by configured aliases/API keys/rules (gateway.go:356-362 rejects unknown models before this call, and gateway.go:370 enforces the per-key model allowlist); `hits` is swapped and re-created each minute so it cannot grow per rule deletion (quota.go:85-86); `Server.lastUsed` (gateway.go:45) is also never pruned but is bounded by API key count; Redis limiter path is TTL-clean (redis_limiter.go:96-97).
